A summary written in technical system terms (internal object IDs, raw field names) for precision

hints: The goal is answering 'does this look right' in the first few seconds, with detail available on demand — not maximum information or maximum speed alone.
A summary a reviewer can't parse quickly (raw internal IDs) fails the same test as a raw dump, just in a different way.
explanation: The lesson's design goal is a reviewer being able to evaluate 'does this look right' from a short summary and flag-reason in the time they realistically have, with full detail available to drill into if something looks off — this is the middle ground between the two failure modes: a raw dump that buries the decision, and a context-free yes/no that removes the ability to evaluate anything at all. A summary written in technical system terms rather than something a human reviewer can parse at a glance repeats the same underlying mistake as the raw dump, just with less total text.

prompt: True or False: a 94% no-changes-needed approval rate, on its own, is strong evidence that the approval process is working as intended.

config.statement: A 94% no-changes-needed approval rate, on its own, is strong evidence that the approval process is working as intended.
config.rubric: Accepts an answer noting that a high approval rate is equally consistent with a genuinely reliable agent and with reviewers rubber-stamping, and that distinguishing the two requires something else — a seeded test case or a time-distribution check — not the rate alone.

hints: The lesson specifically built an evidence-stack drill around this exact number — what did it conclude about the rate alone?
explanation: False. This lesson's own evidence-stack directly addressed this: a high approval rate is exactly what you'd expect from both a genuinely reliable agent and from reviewers who have started rubber-stamping — the number alone can't distinguish the two. Real evidence requires something more targeted, like a deliberately seeded bad request (with reviewer awareness) to check whether it actually gets caught, or a look at whether approval times vary meaningfully with request complexity rather than clustering suspiciously fast and uniform.

prompt: Order these from LEAST to MOST likely to function as a real kill switch during an actual incident, based on this lesson.

items: A configuration change requiring a full redeploy and elevated production access
An approval-gated change ticket that a senior engineer has to review and merge
A single write to a shared flag store, checked at the start of every run, with on-call-rotation-wide access

hints: Rank by how many steps and how much special access stand between 'someone decides to stop it' and 'it's actually stopped.'
The lesson's actual working example was a single flag check at the top of the run function — how far is each option from that?
explanation: The full redeploy option is the slowest and most access-gated — this is literally the failure mode from the lesson's opening incident. An approval-gated change ticket is faster than a redeploy but still routes through a review-and-merge process with its own latency and access requirements. The single flag write, checked at the start of every run and reachable by the whole on-call rotation, matches the lesson's actual working `KillSwitch` design — fewest steps, least gated, fastest to take effect.

prompt: Your team's kill switch is fast and simple (a single database write, checked at run start) but only the two most senior backend engineers have write access to that database table. Is this kill switch design finished? What would you check or change?
hints: Fast and simple solves one half of the problem this lesson raised — which half is still unaddressed?
Recall the Saturday-night scenario in this lesson — what specifically went wrong there, given a technically fast switch?
explanation: No, this isn't finished — it repeats exactly the access half of the failure this lesson described: a fast, well-designed switch that only two named people can reach is still a single point of failure if both are unavailable during a real incident. What to check: does the entire on-call rotation, not just two senior engineers, have the access needed to trigger it? What to change, if not: widen access to match real on-call coverage, with every trigger logged with who and why so the wider access remains individually accountable, rather than assuming two senior people will always be reachable.

prompt: A bank asks a team to prove a disputed refund-approval record wasn't edited after the fact, given that the team has database write access to where it's stored. Which of these actually addresses the bank's specific question?

options.text: A hash-chained log where altering a past entry breaks a mathematically verifiable chain, ideally checkpointed somewhere outside the team's own write access
A more detailed trace of the original customer message and agent reasoning
A written statement from the team affirming the record wasn't edited
Restricting database write access to a single trusted senior engineer

hints: The bank's question is specifically about provability to someone who doesn't have to trust the team, not about the trace's content or the team's word.
Restricting access to one person is still 'trust us,' just with fewer people to trust.
explanation: The bank's question is specifically about proof, not trust — a hash-chained structure makes tampering mathematically detectable by anyone who recomputes the chain, independent of whether they trust the team, which is exactly the standard being asked for. More trace detail doesn't address provability at all. A written affirmation is just an assertion, not proof. Restricting access to one senior engineer still requires trusting that person not to alter the record — it narrows who has to be trusted, but doesn't remove the need to trust someone with write access, which is precisely what the bank's question was probing.

prompt: True or False: since tamper-evident, hash-chained logging is a strong safety mechanism, it should be applied to every trace entry an agent produces, including read-only queries and unsent drafts.

config.statement: Since tamper-evident, hash-chained logging is a strong safety mechanism, it should be applied to every trace entry an agent produces, including read-only queries and unsent drafts.
config.rubric: Accepts an answer noting that hash-chained logging is worth its engineering cost specifically for irreversible/external/high-stakes actions where a real dispute is plausible, and that read-only or unsent-only actions have nothing to dispute, making the added rigor cost without a matching benefit.

hints: This lesson explicitly addressed applying this everywhere versus selectively — what did it conclude, and why?
explanation: False. This lesson's second pod argued directly against this — tamper-evident logging is worth its real engineering cost specifically for irreversible, external, or high-stakes actions where a genuine dispute is plausible (refunds, deletions, anything sent externally). A read-only query or an unsent draft has no external effect and nothing anyone would need to dispute or prove — applying the same rigor there is cost without a matching benefit, the same proportionality judgment made elsewhere in this track about not applying the heaviest available control uniformly regardless of actual risk.

prompt: A user grants a scheduling agent access to 'manage my calendar.' The agent, within that literal access, starts auto-declining meetings it judges low-priority on the user's behalf. What's the core issue, per this lesson?

options.text: 'Manage my calendar' as a broad natural-language grant was treated as license for any action within that access, rather than being scoped to the specific actions the user actually consented to
The agent's judgment about which meetings are low-priority must have been technically inaccurate
Calendar access should never be granted to any agent under any circumstances
The user should have specified every unwanted action in advance to avoid this

hints: This is structurally the same failure as the inbox-handling example from this lesson — what was the actual gap there?
The lesson explicitly argued against putting the burden on the user to enumerate everything they don't want.
explanation: This is the same consent-versus-access gap as the lesson's inbox example: 'manage my calendar' as a technical grant is broader than what the user specifically consented to, and the agent operating at the edge of what's technically permitted (rather than what was actually authorized) produced an action — auto-declining meetings — the user never actually wanted. The fix isn't 'never grant calendar access' (too broad a conclusion) or 'the user should have listed every exception' (the lesson explicitly rejected putting this burden on the user) — it's scoping the delegation to specific, named actions with unlisted ones defaulting to off.

prompt: A user disputes an action their delegated agent took weeks ago, and the team's only record is a permission flag with no timestamp or plain-language description of what was actually granted. Propose what the delegation-recording system should have captured instead, and why each piece matters for resolving a future dispute like this.
hints: What would let a future dispute be settled by checking a record instead of two competing memories?
Consider: what does 'plain-language, recognizable to the user' add over a technical permission flag?
explanation: The system should capture, at the moment of granting: a timestamp (so 'weeks ago' becomes a specific, checkable date), a plain-language description of exactly what was authorized in terms the user would recognize (not just an internal permission flag name), and — at the moment of each action — a link from that specific action back to the specific grant it relied on. Each piece matters for a different reason: the timestamp anchors the dispute to a specific moment instead of vague memory, the plain-language description lets the user actually recognize what they did or didn't agree to (rather than parsing a technical flag), and the action-to-grant link turns 'did the agent do something unauthorized' into a checkable trace instead of a standoff between the agent's records and the user's memory.

prompt: An agent has a tool that posts comments to an internal (not public) project-tracking ticket, fully editable and deletable afterward by any team member. Should this action require approval, per this module's reversibility test?

options.text: No — it's genuinely, cheaply, and quickly reversible by any team member, unlike an external or public action
Yes — any action an agent takes on behalf of a team should always require approval
Yes — because it's a written record, all written records require approval regardless of context
No — approval is never needed for internal-facing actions of any kind

hints: Apply the specific test: can this be undone cheaply and quickly by someone with normal access, or does undoing it require a slow, gated process?
Compare this to the public-blog-post example from lesson one — what's the key difference?
explanation: This clears the reversibility bar cleanly — an internal comment, editable or deletable by any team member with normal access, costs essentially nothing to undo if wrong. This is meaningfully different from a public blog post (visible externally the moment it's posted) or a refund (money already moved) — not every internal-facing or even 'written' action is automatically irreversible; the specific, practical cost of undoing it is what determines the answer, not a blanket rule about internal actions or written records.

prompt: Order these steps for designing an approval gate for a new high-stakes agent action, from first to last.

items: Confirm the action is genuinely, practically irreversible or high-stakes enough to warrant gating
Design the approval request format to surface the specific decision, why it was flagged, and relevant confidence/context
Test the request against a deliberately bad or ambiguous case to confirm a reviewer could actually catch it
Monitor real approval patterns over time (rate, timing) to detect drift toward rubber-stamping

hints: You need to know an action deserves gating before designing what the gate looks like.
Testing against a bad case and monitoring over time are both verification steps, but one happens before launch and one happens continuously after.
explanation: Confirming the action genuinely needs gating comes first, since not everything does. Designing the request format follows, aimed at making the decision reviewable. Testing against a deliberately bad case verifies the design actually works before relying on it in production. Ongoing monitoring for drift toward rubber-stamping is a continuous check after launch, since a gate that worked at launch can still degrade in practice over time.

prompt: Sort each incident into the control (reversibility judgment, approval design, kill switch, auditability, or delegation scoping) it's mainly a failure of.

items.text: A refund tool executes directly from the agent's decision with no human checkpoint for an irreversible money-moving action
A reviewer approves a 40-line raw context dump in three seconds without reading past line 3
An agent is stopped only six minutes after an incident starts, because stopping it requires a full redeploy
A team can't prove to an external party that a disputed record wasn't edited after the fact
An agent auto-replies to emails on a user's behalf, technically within its granted access but never actually wanted

hints: Match each incident to the specific lesson it traces back to, not just 'something went wrong with safety.'
The redeploy-gated stop and the raw-dump approval look similar (both are process problems) but trace to different lessons.
explanation: Each incident traces to a specific lesson: the unchecked refund execution to a missing reversibility gate (lesson one); the unread approval request to poor approval-request design (lesson two); the six-minute redeploy-gated stop to a kill switch that isn't actually fast and reachable (lesson three); the unprovable record to missing tamper-evidence (lesson four); the unwanted auto-reply to scope defined by technical access rather than actual consent (lesson five).

prompt: True or False: an agent operating strictly within the technical permissions it was granted can never violate what a person actually wanted.

config.statement: An agent operating strictly within the technical permissions it was granted can never violate what a person actually wanted.
config.rubric: Accepts an answer citing the inbox or calendar example — technical access and actual consent are different things, and staying within technical permission doesn't guarantee staying within what was actually wanted.

hints: Recall the inbox auto-reply and calendar auto-decline examples from this lesson — were either of those outside the agent's technical permissions?
explanation: False. Both this lesson's examples — the inbox agent auto-replying, the calendar agent auto-declining meetings — stayed strictly within their technically granted access and still did something the person never actually wanted. Technical permission and actual consent are different things; a broad grant like 'handle my inbox' or 'manage my calendar' is often interpreted more expansively than the person meant, which is exactly why this lesson argued for scoping delegation at the level of specific named actions rather than relying on technical access as a proxy for what was actually authorized.

prompt: Match each symptom to its most likely root cause from this module's five lessons.

pairs.left: A $4,200 refund executes immediately from a misread customer message with no human checkpoint
pairs.right: No approval gate on an irreversible, money-moving action

pairs.left: A reviewer approves every request in under 10 seconds without reading the details
pairs.right: Approval request buries the decision in irrelevant raw detail

pairs.left: Nine repeated mistakes happen in the six minutes before an agent is finally stopped
pairs.right: Kill switch requires a slow, access-gated deploy process instead of a fast runtime check

pairs.left: A user disputes an action and neither side can point to a record that settles it
pairs.right: No specific, timestamped, plain-language consent record tied to that action

hints: Match each visible symptom to the specific missing mechanism from this module's five lessons, as in previous modules' matching drills.
The six-minute delay and the unread approval request are both 'the approval/control step failed' but trace to different specific causes.
explanation: Each symptom traces to a specific gap: the unchecked $4,200 refund to a missing approval gate on an irreversible action (lesson one); the rubber-stamped approvals to a request design that buries the decision (lesson two); the nine repeated mistakes to a kill switch that isn't fast and reachable (lesson three); the unresolvable dispute to a missing specific consent record (lesson five).

prompt: A team wants to know if their approval process still works after six months in production. Which check, from this module, would actually tell them something useful, as opposed to looking reassuring without being informative?

options.text: Periodically seed a deliberately wrong test case into the approval queue, with reviewer awareness, and check whether it's caught
Check that the overall approval rate hasn't changed much from launch
Survey reviewers on whether they feel confident in their own review process
Confirm the approval UI hasn't had any bugs reported in the last month

hints: This module's approval-design lesson directly compared these options for exactly this purpose — which one actually distinguishes genuine reliability from rubber-stamping?
An unchanged approval rate is consistent with both a healthy process and a degraded one, same as the original 94% example.
explanation: A seeded test case, with reviewers aware this practice exists, is the one check that actually distinguishes a genuinely functioning approval process from one that's degraded into rubber-stamping — either the bad case gets caught or it doesn't, which is real evidence. An unchanged approval rate is ambiguous by the same logic as the original 94% example — a stable rate is consistent with both a healthy and a degraded process. A self-reported confidence survey and a bug-report count both measure something other than whether reviewers are actually catching real problems.

prompt: You're designing human-in-the-loop controls for an agent that can modify a shared internal wiki (edits are visible immediately to the whole company, with full edit history and one-click revert available to any editor). Walk through, in a few sentences each, whether this needs an approval gate, a kill switch, tamper-evident auditing, and delegation scoping — and why or why not for each.
hints: Apply the reversibility test specifically — one-click revert available to anyone is a meaningfully different situation from the refund or database-deletion examples.
Not every control from this module is needed for every agent — which ones are actually load-bearing here, and which would be disproportionate?
explanation: A reasonable walkthrough: approval gate — probably not required as a hard blocker, since one-click revert by any editor makes this genuinely, cheaply reversible (unlike the refund or four-hour-restore examples), though a lighter-weight notification-after-the-fact could still be reasonable. Kill switch — still worth having regardless of reversibility, since a malfunctioning agent making many bad edits quickly is still disruptive even if each edit is individually revertible; the value here is stopping the pattern, not any single edit. Tamper-evident auditing — not really needed at the hash-chain level, since edit history with full revert capability is itself already a reasonably auditable, non-disputed record for this kind of internal, low-stakes content. Delegation scoping — still matters if this agent acts on behalf of specific users rather than as its own system identity, to keep 'what a person authorized this agent to edit' distinguishable from 'what the agent decided to edit.'

prompt: Order these from the point earliest in an agent's action lifecycle to latest where each control this module covered would actually engage.

items: Delegation scope check — is this action type authorized for this specific user's grant at all
Reversibility/approval gate — does this specific action need a human checkpoint before executing
Kill switch check — is the system allowed to start or continue running at all right now
Audit log entry — record what was decided and done, provably, after the action completes

hints: The kill switch is checked at the very start of a run, before anything about the specific action is even evaluated.
Scope has to be confirmed before deciding whether that specific, now-known-to-be-authorized action also needs approval.
The audit record is necessarily the last of these, since it records what actually happened.
explanation: The kill switch is checked first, at the very start of the run, before any action-specific logic runs at all — if it's active, nothing else here matters. Delegation scope is checked next, for the specific action being considered, since you need to know an action is even authorized before deciding whether it also needs approval. The approval/reversibility gate comes next, for actions that are in-scope but still need a human checkpoint given their reversibility. The audit log entry is last, since it records what was actually decided and done, which by definition happens after the action completes.

prompt: Sort each scenario into the type of drift it best illustrates.

categories: Behavioral drift on the far side

items.text: A support agent's underlying question patterns shift toward a new product line nobody trained it heavily on
A news site an agent scrapes redesigns its page and moves the headline into a differently-named HTML element
A partner API a pricing agent calls starts rate-limiting far more aggressively than it used to, without any documented schema change
items.category: Behavioral drift on the far side

items.text: A document-parsing agent's input format shifts from mostly PDFs to mostly scanned images over several months

hints: Structural drift is about the shape of data changing; distributional drift is about the kind of input shifting; behavioral drift is about something's actual behavior changing without a shape change.
The rate-limiting example doesn't change any field's shape — it changes how the API behaves under the same request pattern.
explanation: The HTML redesign is a shape change to a specific structural element — structural drift. The shift toward a new product line and the shift from PDFs to scanned images are both changes in the kind of input arriving, not in any single source's shape — distributional drift. The more aggressive rate-limiting is a behavioral change on the far side of a dependency, with no documented schema or structural change at all — the trickiest kind to catch from a schema diff alone.

prompt: Your team's only current monitoring for an agent is 'did the tool call return HTTP 200.' Based on this lesson, what's the specific blind spot this leaves, and what would you add?
hints: The pricing-agent scenario in this lesson had a tool call that succeeded (in the HTTP sense) while returning wrong data — what's the general version of that gap?
What kind of check specifically distinguishes 'the call succeeded' from 'the call returned something correct'?
explanation: HTTP 200 only confirms the request was received and a response was returned — it says nothing about whether the response's content is actually correct, which is exactly the blind spot that let the pricing-agent scenario run for five weeks undetected. The addition this lesson argues for: a periodic re-run of a small, fixed eval set with known-correct answers, checked against the live system, so a correctness regression shows up as a dropping accuracy number even while every individual call keeps returning a clean 200.

prompt: A model provider announces a deprecation with 90 days' notice. Which response best matches this lesson's guidance?

options.text: Start a migration process immediately: run the eval set against the new version within the first two weeks, leaving real time to fix any regressions found before the deadline
Wait until close to the deadline, since the model provider will likely extend it anyway
Swap immediately with no testing, since 90 days is plenty of buffer regardless of what's found
Ignore the deprecation until the old version actually stops responding

hints: This lesson's core argument is about when the real work (fixing regressions) happens, not just whether the swap happens before the deadline.
90 days of buffer only helps if it's actually used for the step that takes real time — finding and fixing regressions.
explanation: Starting immediately, with the eval-set comparison happening early, is what actually uses the 90-day window for its real purpose — leaving time for the step this lesson identified as the critical bottleneck: fixing whatever regressions the evaluation reveals. Waiting for a possible extension gambles on something outside the team's control. Swapping immediately with no testing skips the actual verification this lesson is built around. Ignoring the deprecation converts a planned migration into a forced, last-minute one once the old version actually stops working.

prompt: True or False: an aggregate eval score within a couple of percentage points of baseline is sufficient evidence that a model migration is safe to fully ship.

config.statement: An aggregate eval score within a couple of percentage points of baseline is sufficient evidence that a model migration is safe to fully ship.
config.rubric: Accepts an answer citing the per-category regression example — a small aggregate drop can hide a severe regression in an underrepresented category, so the aggregate alone isn't sufficient evidence.

hints: Recall the 93%-to-91% example in this lesson — was that aggregate number actually telling the whole story?
explanation: False. This lesson's own example showed a 93%-to-91% aggregate drop — small and seemingly acceptable — hiding a specific category's collapse from 89% to 61%, nearly completely absorbed by the overall average because that category was a small slice of the eval set. A migration decision needs the per-category breakdown specifically because an aggregate number close to baseline is consistent with both 'nothing regressed' and 'one category collapsed but got averaged away' — only the granular view distinguishes the two.

prompt: Order these from least to most resilient response to an upstream API making a previously-required field optional.

items: Code assumes the field always exists; an unhandled exception crashes the run when it's missing
Code checks for the field's presence and logs a warning, but otherwise proceeds with degraded/unknown confidence
A scheduled contract test independently checks the field's presence against the live API before any real run depends on it

hints: Rank by how early the problem is caught, and how gracefully the system handles it once caught.
The first option is literally what happened in this lesson's incident; the last is what would have caught it before it ever reached a real customer run.
explanation: The unhandled-exception case is the least resilient — it's the actual incident this lesson describes, where a normal upstream change became a production crash. An explicit, logged check is more resilient — it turns the same event into a handled, debuggable case rather than a crash, but only after the fact, during a real run. A scheduled contract test is the most resilient — it catches the exact same change independently, on its own schedule, before it ever affects a real customer-facing run.

prompt: A team's integration test for a payment API asserts `response.status_code == 200`. Based on this lesson, what's the main gap in this test as a way to catch a breaking contract change?

options.text: It doesn't check the response's actual structure or the presence of fields the code depends on — a 200 status with a changed or missing field would still pass
It should test against a mock instead of the real API
The test runs too infrequently to be useful
Status code checks are never useful for any kind of API testing

hints: Recall the shipping-API test example — 'response is not None' passed throughout the entire incident. Is a status code check meaningfully different from that?
A 200 status code tells you the request succeeded at the HTTP level — does it tell you anything about the response body's shape?
explanation: A 200 status code is exactly the same category of shallow check as 'response is not None' in this lesson's spot-flaw example — it confirms the request succeeded at the transport level, but says nothing about whether the response body still has the shape the code depends on. A real contract test needs to check specific fields' presence and type, not just that a response with a success status arrived. Mocking versus hitting the real API and test frequency are both real, separate considerations, but neither is the specific gap illustrated here — the gap is what the assertion actually checks.

prompt: A team's 'always' tier maintenance check includes reviewing 30 days of flagged conversations in detail, estimated at 40 minutes. Based on this lesson, what's wrong with this design?

options.text: A 40-minute task is too heavy for an 'always' tier meant to survive a genuinely bad week — it belongs in the 'full' tier instead
Reviewing flagged conversations is never a valuable maintenance activity
30 days is too short a review window for any maintenance check
Nothing is wrong — as long as it's valuable, it belongs in the always tier

hints: This is the exact scenario from this lesson's second pod — what did the lesson conclude about 'valuable' versus 'belongs in the always tier'?
The whole point of the always tier is surviving a week with almost no discretionary time — does 40 minutes fit that?
explanation: This repeats the exact mistake from this lesson's second pod: a genuinely valuable task (like the 45-minute conversation review debated there) still doesn't belong in the 'always' tier if it's too heavy to survive a genuinely bad week — value and always-tier eligibility are different questions. The task itself isn't wrong to do; it belongs in the 'full' tier, which is allowed to slip during a bad month without the whole maintenance system collapsing to nothing.

prompt: You're designing the 'always' tier for a coding agent that can open pull requests. List two or three specific checks you'd include, and explain why each one specifically belongs in the cheap, always-survives-a-bad-week tier rather than the fuller tier.
hints: The always tier is for checks whose silent failure would be costly, kept cheap enough to always happen — what's the coding-agent equivalent of the kill-switch and budget checks from this lesson's example?
Ask, for each candidate check: could this genuinely be done in a couple of minutes, or does it require real, focused time?
explanation: Reasonable always-tier candidates for a coding agent: (1) confirm the agent's credential/token is still valid and correctly scoped (a quick check, and a silently expired or over-scoped token is a costly failure to miss); (2) confirm the kill switch or PR-approval gate is still reachable and functioning (mirrors the previous module's kill-switch reachability check — cheap to verify, costly if silently broken); (3) skim the count and outcome of PRs opened in the last week for any that got auto-merged without review, which would indicate an approval gate failure. Each belongs in the always tier specifically because it's a quick, near-binary check (working or not) rather than something requiring real judgment or focused time, and each guards against a failure mode that would be expensive precisely because it's silent.

prompt: True or False: if every individual maintenance fix on an agent was worth doing at the time, the cumulative decision to keep maintaining it must also be worth it.

config.statement: If every individual maintenance fix on an agent was worth doing at the time, the cumulative decision to keep maintaining it must also be worth it.
config.rubric: Accepts an answer noting that per-incident and cumulative evaluations are different questions — each fix being locally reasonable doesn't mean the total pattern, evaluated as a whole, is still the best use of ongoing investment.

hints: Recall the eighteen-month document-classification agent example — was any single patch along the way actually a bad call?
explanation: False. This is exactly the trap this lesson describes — 'is this specific fix worth doing right now' is almost always yes in isolation (a fix is usually cheap compared to the failure it prevents), but that per-incident question never automatically answers the different, cumulative question of whether eighteen months of ongoing investment is still the best use of that time compared to alternatives. A system can be individually-reasonable-to-patch at every single incident while the aggregate pattern genuinely deserves a fresh, deliberate look.

prompt: Propose specific, numeric sunset criteria for an internal reporting agent that costs roughly 3 engineering hours a month to maintain on average, spiking occasionally after a data-source change. What threshold and time window would you set, and why?
hints: The lesson's example used a per-quarter hour threshold and required multiple consecutive quarters over it, to avoid triggering on one unlucky spike.
3 hours/month average means about 9 hours/quarter under normal conditions — what threshold would distinguish 'a bad quarter' from 'a genuine new normal'?
explanation: A reasonable proposal: a per-quarter maintenance-hours threshold somewhat above the normal baseline — e.g. 20-25 hours/quarter (roughly 2.5x the ~9 hour/quarter baseline) — combined with a requirement of at least two consecutive quarters over that threshold before triggering a deliberate review, mirroring this lesson's own example. The margin above baseline matters so one unusually bad quarter (a single larger data-source migration, say) doesn't trigger an unnecessary review; requiring consecutive quarters distinguishes a genuine sustained shift in maintenance cost from a one-off spike, the same distinction the lesson's own criteria were built to make.

prompt: An agent's accuracy on a fixed weekly eval set drops from 94% to 71% over three weeks, with zero code changes and no error-rate increase in the logs. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: Some external dependency (a data source, an API's behavior) has drifted, and the error-rate-only monitoring isn't catching it because calls are still 'succeeding' while returning increasingly wrong results
The eval set itself must be broken, since real accuracy can't drop without a code change
This must be normal noise and not worth investigating
The model provider silently swapped which model responds to the pinned version string

hints: This is the exact shape of this module's opening scenario — a real correctness metric dropping while the error-based monitoring stays flat.
A 23-point drop over three weeks with a stable error rate is a specific, large signal — not noise.
explanation: A real accuracy drop with zero code changes and a flat error rate matches exactly the drift pattern this module opened with — an external dependency has likely changed in a way that produces wrong-but-successful results, invisible to error-rate monitoring. A 23-point drop over three weeks is a large, specific signal, not noise to dismiss. The eval set being broken is possible but far less likely than genuine drift given the specific, gradual pattern described, and there's no indication here of a provider-side model swap specifically, as opposed to any of several possible drift sources.

prompt: Order these steps for responding to a model provider's deprecation announcement, from first to last.

items: Run the existing eval set against the new model version
Compare results per-category against the current baseline, not just the aggregate score
Fix any regressions found in specific categories
Canary the new version to a small percentage of real traffic before full cutover

hints: You need eval results before you can compare anything.
Fixing has to happen after regressions are identified at the category level, not just after seeing an aggregate number.
explanation: Running the eval set against the new version comes first, since nothing else is possible without results to examine. Comparing per-category, not just in aggregate, is next, since that's what actually reveals whether something regressed (the aggregate alone can hide it, as this module's lesson two showed). Fixing regressions follows identification. Canarying to real traffic is the final, cautious step before full cutover, providing a real-world check beyond the eval set alone.

Asking whoever built the agent originally whether they still believe in it
Waiting for a single, especially bad incident to force the question
Assuming any agent still technically running must still be worth running

Asking the original builder or waiting for a single bad incident both skip the cumulative-tracking step this lesson argued for.
explanation: A maintenance log tracked over time, reviewed on a recurring schedule, is what actually makes the cumulative cost visible and answerable with real numbers — exactly what was missing in the eighteen-month example until someone finally added it up. Asking the original builder surfaces attachment and opinion, not evidence. prompt: You inherit an agent someone else built two years ago, with no documentation about its dependencies, no maintenance log, and no sunset criteria. Walk through, in a few sentences each, what you'd do first to bring it in line with this module's practices, and in what order.
hints: You can't design sunset criteria or a maintenance routine for risks you haven't identified yet — what has to come first?
Consider what's cheapest and most urgent to establish versus what can follow once the basics are in place.
explanation: A reasonable order: first, map the agent's actual external dependencies (model version, APIs, data sources) since nothing else in this module can be done without knowing what could drift or break (lesson one and three's foundation). Second, establish basic correctness monitoring beyond success/error rates — even a small fixed eval set re-run periodically is better than nothing, to start catching drift going forward rather than waiting for the next surprise. Third, start a maintenance log now, even with no historical data, so a cumulative view starts accumulating from this point forward rather than staying invisible indefinitely. Fourth, once a few months of real maintenance data exist, set sunset criteria grounded in that real cost rather than a guess made on day one with no data at all — sunset criteria set too early, before any real cost data exists, would just be another guess dressed up as a number.
